Prealgebra · Lesson 2.1

Squares and Cubes

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Squaring a number means multiplying it by itself, written b2b2 and read as “b squared.” A product like 3×53×5 counts a grid with 3 rows and 5 columns, so 5252 counts a grid with 5 rows and 5 columns, an actual square. That square picture explains most of the shortcuts in this lesson.

Problem
Here are the first six perfect squares. 12=1,22=4,32=9,42=16,52=25,62=3612=1,22=4,32=9,42=16,52=25,62=36 Look at how much each square grows over the one before it, then use that growth pattern to predict 8282 without multiplying 8×88×8 directly.
Show a hint
  • The growth from one square to the next goes 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, all odd numbers increasing by 2. What should the next two terms in that list be?
Show the full solution
The growth from each square to the next is 3,5,7,9,11,…3,5,7,9,11,…, the odd numbers, each one 2 more than the last. The next two terms are 13 and 15. So 72=36+13=4972=36+13=49, and 82=49+15=64.82=49+15=64​. Every step from one perfect square to the next adds the next odd number.

A square is what you get from two copies of a number multiplied together. Use three copies and you get a cube. Where b2b2 counted the cells of a flat square, b3b3 counts the little cubes packed inside a solid one.

Problem
Stack unit cubes into a solid block. One cube along each edge is just 11 cube, two along each edge make 88, three along each edge make 2727. How many unit cubes are in a block that is 44 along each edge?
Show a hint
  • Each flat layer is a 4×4=164×4=16 square of cubes, and the block is 44 layers tall.
Show the full solution
Each layer is a 4×4=164×4=16 square of unit cubes, and there are 44 such layers stacked up. 4×4×4=644×4×4=64​ That count is 4343, and the list 1,8,27,641,8,27,64 is the start of the perfect cubes.
Key idea
For any number bb, the square b2b2 is b×bb×b and the cube b3b3 is b×b×bb×b×b. When bb is a whole number these are the perfect squares 0,1,4,9,16,25,…0,1,4,9,16,25,… and the perfect cubes 0,1,8,27,64,125,…0,1,8,27,64,125,… Geometrically b2b2 counts the cells in a bb-by-bb square and b3b3 counts the unit cubes in a bb-by-bb-by-bb cube. Cubes grow much faster than squares, since each step multiplies by bb one extra time.
Problem
Compute 2×322×32. Is it 2×(32)2×(32) or (2×3)2(2×3)2? Those give different values, 18 and 36, so the placement of the exponent matters.
Show a hint
  • An exponent attaches only to the symbol written directly beneath it, not to anything sitting in front of it.
Show the full solution
The exponent sits on the 33, so evaluate 3232 first. 2×32=2×9=182×32=2×9=18​ An exponent applies only to the symbol written directly beneath it, never to anything in front of it. Squaring the whole 2×32×3 needs parentheses, and (2×3)2=36(2×3)2=36 is a different expression.
Problem
Two students evaluate −52−52. One says −25−25 and the other says 2525. An exponent grips just the base written beneath it, and only one student used that rule. Find the value of (−5)2(−5)2 and the value of −52−52, then subtract the second from the first.
Show a hint
  • In −52−52, is the minus sign part of the base, or is it applied after the squaring? Compare −52−52 with −1×52−1×52.
  • In (−5)2(−5)2 the parentheses put the negative inside the base, so the product is (−5)×(−5)(−5)×(−5). Then remember that subtracting a negative number adds.
Show the full solution
(−5)2−(−52)=25−(−25)=50(−5)2−(−52)=25−(−25)=50​ The exponent in −52−52 sits on the 55 alone, so the minus sign is applied last and −52=−(52)=−25−52=−(52)=−25. The student who said −25−25 is right. Parentheses change the base itself, so (−5)2=(−5)×(−5)=25(−5)2=(−5)×(−5)=25. Same digits, opposite signs, and subtracting the negative one leaves 25+25=5025+25=50.
Problem
Compute (−2)3(−2)3. Then compute −23−23. With squares these two came out opposite, since (−2)2=4(−2)2=4 but −22=−4−22=−4. What happens this time?
Show a hint
  • (−2)3=(−2)(−2)(−2)(−2)3=(−2)(−2)(−2). Multiply the first two, then bring in the third.
  • An exponent still binds only to its own base, so −23−23 means −(23)−(23).
Show the full solution
Multiply the three factors of (−2)3(−2)3 one at a time. (−2)(−2)=4(−2)(−2)=4, then 4×(−2)=−84×(−2)=−8. And −23=−(23)=−8−23=−(23)=−8 as well, since the exponent binds only to the 22. Both come out to −8.−8​. This time the two expressions are equal, not opposite. Three negative factors pair off with one left over, so the cube of a negative stays negative.
Problem
Evaluate 2x2−x2x2−x when x=−3x=−3.
Show a hint
  • Substitute −3−3 for xx and put parentheses around it everywhere it appears, so the expression becomes 2(−3)2−(−3)2(−3)2−(−3).
Show the full solution
Substitute x=−3x=−3, keeping it inside parentheses. 2(−3)2−(−3)2(−3)2−(−3) The exponent applies to the whole parenthesized −3−3, so (−3)2=9(−3)2=9. 2(9)−(−3)=18+3=212(9)−(−3)=18+3=21​ Dropping the parentheses and writing 2×−322×−32 would turn the first piece into −2×9=−18−2×9=−18, a different and wrong expression.
Key idea
Evaluate powers after parentheses but before multiplication, division, addition, and subtraction. An exponent applies only to the base written directly beneath it. So −an=−(an)−an=−(an), while (−a)n(−a)n raises the negative itself. The two are opposite when nn is even, so (−5)2=25(−5)2=25 but −52=−25−52=−25. They are equal when nn is odd, so (−2)3=−23=−8(−2)3=−23=−8.

Squares and cubes also split across multiplication and division. That split turns awkward products into easy ones, and the next few problems build the rule.

Problem
Compute 6262 directly. Then compute it a second way: write 6=2×36=2×3, expand (2×3)×(2×3)(2×3)×(2×3) into four factors, and use the reordering freedom from Chapter 1 to group the two 2's together and the two 3's together. Do the two methods agree, and what does the regrouped form become?
Show a hint
  • After regrouping, the four factors split into 2×22×2 and 3×33×3, which are 2222 and 3232.
Show the full solution
Directly, 62=3662=36. Expanding the second way, (2×3)×(2×3)=2×3×2×3(2×3)×(2×3)=2×3×2×3 Reordering and regrouping these four factors gives (2×2)×(3×3)=22×32=4×9=36(2×2)×(3×3)=22×32=4×9=36​ Both routes agree, and along the way (2×3)2(2×3)2 turned into 22×3222×32. Squaring a product is the same as squaring each factor and multiplying the results.
Problem
Compute 23×5323×53 without cubing either number on its own first.
Show a hint
  • A cube distributes over a product, so 23×53=(2×5)323×53=(2×5)3.
Show the full solution
Cubing distributes over multiplication, so gather the bases before cubing. 23×53=(2×5)3=103=100023×53=(2×5)3=103=1000​ The same pairing that turned an awkward product into a round number for squares works again for cubes.
Problem
Compute 252×42252×42 without ever multiplying two multi-digit numbers together.
Show a hint
  • The pairing trick from Chapter 1 is back. What is 25×425×4?
Show the full solution
Since a2b2=(ab)2a2b2=(ab)2, 252×42=(25×4)2=1002=10000252×42=(25×4)2=1002=10000​ The same pairing that turned 25×425×4 into a clean 100100 now turns two awkward squares into one easy one.
Key idea
Back at the start of this lesson, each perfect square was an odd number more than the one before it, exactly 2n+12n+1 more. That same pattern is a fast way to square a number next to a round one.

Back at the start of this lesson, the jump from one perfect square to the next was always an odd number, 2n+12n+1 more than the square before it. That pattern is a shortcut for squaring in your head.

Key idea
(n+1)2=n2+2n+1(n+1)2=n2+2n+1. To square a number one more than a round nn, square nn, add twice nn, then add 11. The figure shows why. The bigger square is the old nn-by-nn square plus two strips of length nn plus one corner cell. Run it backward, (n−1)2=n2−2n+1(n−1)2=n2−2n+1, to square a number just below a round one. This is also why consecutive perfect squares differ by the odd number 2n+12n+1.
Problem
Use (n+1)2=n2+2n+1(n+1)2=n2+2n+1 to compute 412412 without multiplying two 2-digit numbers.
Show a hint
  • Let n=40n=40, a very friendly number. What are n2n2, 2n2n, and the final +1+1?
Show the full solution
Take n=40n=40. Then n2=1600n2=1600 and 2n=802n=80. 412=1600+80+1=1681412=1600+80+1=1681​ Every piece is a number you can add in your head.
Problem
The identity also runs in reverse. If n=m+1n=m+1, then n2=m2+2m+1n2=m2+2m+1, which rearranges to (n−1)2=n2−2n+1(n−1)2=n2−2n+1 (writing m=n−1m=n−1). Use this reversed identity to compute 992992 from the friendly number 100100.
Show a hint
  • Let n=100n=100, so 992=(n−1)2=n2−2n+1992=(n−1)2=n2−2n+1.
Show the full solution
Take n=100n=100. Then n2=10000n2=10000 and 2n=2002n=200. 992=10000−200+1=9801992=10000−200+1=9801​ One identity, run forward for a number just above a round number and run backward for a number just below one.
Problem
Compute 123÷33123÷33 without ever finding 123123.
Show a hint
  • A cube distributes over division, so 123÷33=(12÷3)3123÷33=(12÷3)3.
Show the full solution
Since (ab)3=a3b3(ba​)3=b3a3​, read the division with the cube on the outside. 123÷33=(12÷3)3=43=64123÷33=(12÷3)3=43=64​ One small cube, 4343, in place of a four-digit division.

Practice these ideas

Practice
A square garden is 4040 tiles along each side. The owner widens it to 4141 tiles along each side. Find how many tiles get added, without ever computing 402402 or 412412.
Show the solution
Going from a 4040-by-4040 square out to 4141-by-4141 wraps an L-shaped gnomon around the old garden. The strip is two sides of length 4040 plus the single corner where they meet, so it holds 2×40+1=812×40+1=81​ tiles. That is the jump 412−402412−402, and it came out odd, the way every step between consecutive squares does.
Practice
Two perfect squares sit side by side on the staircase of squares, and the larger is exactly 159159 more than the smaller. The two numbers being squared are whole numbers one apart. Find the larger of those two numbers.
Show the solution
The step from one perfect square to the next is the gnomon 2n+12n+1, where nn is the smaller number being squared. Here that step is 159159, so 2n+1=1592n+1=159. Peeling off the 11 leaves 2n=1582n=158, and half of 158158 is n=79n=79. The two squares are 792792 and 802802, so the larger number being squared is 8080​. As a check, 802−792=2×79+1=159802−792=2×79+1=159.
Practice
You handled both of those without squaring anything. The step between one perfect square and the next is always the odd number 2n+12n+1, the gnomon strip wrapped around the smaller square. Read it forward to get the jump. Read it backward to get the side.
Practice
Add the odd numbers from 1111 up to 3939. 11+13+15+⋯+37+3911+13+15+⋯+37+39 The first nn odd numbers add up to n2n2. Use that twice instead of adding all fifteen terms.
Show the solution
The odd numbers from 11 to 3939 are the first 2020 odds, since 3939 is the twentieth odd number, so they sum to 202=400202=400. The run you want skips the small odds 1,3,5,7,91,3,5,7,9, which are the first 55 odds and sum to 52=2552=25. Trim that front block off. 11+13+⋯+39=202−52=400−25=37511+13+⋯+39=202−52=400−25=375​ A run of consecutive odds is one square with a smaller square sliced off its start.
Practice
A run of odd numbers starting at 11 folds into a single square, because the first nn odds build an nn-by-nn square one gnomon at a time. A run that starts higher up is just that same idea, one square with a smaller square trimmed off the front.
Practice
A cubical crate is packed snug with small cubical boxes, no gaps. The boxes sit 55 across the floor, 55 deep, and the stack is 55 boxes tall. How many small boxes fill one full crate?
Show the solution
Each layer resting on the floor is a 5×5=255×5=25 square of boxes, and 55 such layers stack from bottom to top. 5×5×5=53=1255×5×5=53=125​ A cubical crate packed with cubical boxes always holds a perfect cube of them.
Practice
A square photo has side 44 cm, so its area is 42=1642=16 square cm. A cube-shaped box also has side 44 cm, so its volume is 43=6443=64 cubic cm. Now double every side, sending each to 88 cm. The box's volume grows by more cubic cm than the photo's area grows by square cm. How many more?
Show the solution
Because a square distributes over a product, (2b)2=22b2=4b2(2b)2=22b2=4b2, so doubling the side multiplies the area by 44. The photo goes from 1616 to 82=6482=64, a growth of 4848 square cm. A cube distributes the same way, (2b)3=23b3=8b3(2b)3=23b3=8b3, so doubling the side multiplies the volume by 88. The box goes from 6464 to 83=51283=512, a growth of 448448 cubic cm. The volume outgrew the area by 448−48=400.448−48=400​.
Practice
A square counts a flat area and a cube counts a solid volume, and that one extra dimension is the whole story. Stretch the side and a cube grows more than a square. Double the side and the area climbs by 2222, while the volume climbs by 2323.
Practice
Two expressions go head to head. A=−42+(−3)3B=(−4)2+(−3)2A=−42+(−3)3B=(−4)2+(−3)2 A classmate says they must be equal since they use the same numbers. Evaluate each one, watching every minus sign, and enter the value of the larger.
Show the solution
Take AA one piece at a time. In −42−42 the exponent attaches only to the 44, so −42=−(42)=−16−42=−(42)=−16. And (−3)3(−3)3 cubes a negative, and an odd power keeps the sign, so (−3)3=−27(−3)3=−27. Thus A=−16+(−27)=−43A=−16+(−27)=−43. Now BB. Here (−4)2(−4)2 squares the whole −4−4, and an even power of a negative is positive, so (−4)2=16(−4)2=16, and likewise (−3)2=9(−3)2=9. Thus B=16+9=25B=16+9=25. The two are nowhere near equal. The parentheses flipped two of the four signs, and the larger value is 2525​.
Practice
A detective is handed four numbers and told that exactly one is a perfect square. 3142764008571219000331427640085712190003 She names it in seconds by glancing only at the last digit of each, never computing a square. Which number is the perfect square?
Show the solution
The last digit of b2b2 depends only on the last digit of bb. Running through 02,12,…,9202,12,…,92, the endings that ever appear are 0,1,4,9,6,5,6,9,4,10,1,4,9,6,5,6,9,4,1, so a perfect square can only finish in 0,1,4,5,6,0,1,4,5,6, or 99, never in 2,3,7,2,3,7, or 88. Now scan. 3142731427 ends in 77, 6400864008 ends in 88, and 9000390003 ends in 33, all impossible. Only 5712157121 ends in a legal digit, so it is the square. Indeed 57121=239257121=2392. The answer is 5712157121​.
Practice
A secret two-digit whole number NN is cubed, and only the cube is shown. N3=50653N3=50653 Two clues pin NN with no guessing. The size of the cube traps NN in one narrow band, and the last digit of 5065350653 reveals the last digit of NN outright. Find NN.
Show the solution
First trap NN by size. Since 303=27000303=27000 and 403=64000403=64000, and 5065350653 sits between them, NN is somewhere in the thirties. That still leaves ten numbers, so bring in the last digit. When you cube 00 through 99, the last digits come out 0,1,8,7,4,5,6,3,2,90,1,8,7,4,5,6,3,2,9, every digit exactly once. A cube ending in 33 can only come from a base ending in 77. The one number in the thirties ending in 77 is 3737, and 373=50653373=50653 checks out. So N=37N=37​.
Practice
The last digit of a power leans only on the last digit of the base. For squares that digit blurs several bases together, since 22 and 88 both square to an ending of 44, so it can rule a number out but not pin it down. For cubes every digit appears exactly once, so a cube's last digit fingerprints its base with no doubt at all.
Practice
A machine takes a whole number, squares it, adds twice the number, then adds 11. You feed it 7979, and it prints a single perfect square. Find that square, but do it without multiplying two two-digit numbers. Name the perfect square first, then split it across a friendly product.
Show the solution
The machine builds 792+2×79+1792+2×79+1, which is exactly n2+2n+1n2+2n+1 with n=79n=79. That pattern folds up into (n+1)2(n+1)2, so the output is (79+1)2=802(79+1)2=802. Now dodge squaring 8080 head on. A square distributes over a product, so split the base. 802=(8×10)2=82×102=64×100=6400802=(8×10)2=82×102=64×100=6400​ The expansion collapsed into one square, and that square broke into two easy pieces.
Practice
The signs alternate all the way down this chain of squares. 202−192+182−172+⋯+22−12202−192+182−172+⋯+22−12 Do not square twenty numbers. Group the chain into pairs from the left, turn each pair into something simpler, then add.
Show the solution
Pair the chain from the left, (202−192)+(182−172)+⋯+(22−12)(202−192)+(182−172)+⋯+(22−12). Each pair is a step between two consecutive squares, and that step is the odd number 2n−12n−1. So 202−192=39202−192=39, then 182−172=35182−172=35, on down to 22−12=322−12=3. The ten pairs become the ten odd numbers 39,35,31,27,23,19,15,11,7,339,35,31,27,23,19,15,11,7,3. Add them by matching the ends inward, 39+3=4239+3=42, 35+7=4235+7=42, and so on, which gives five pairs of 4242. 5×42=2105×42=210​
Practice
The holding-hands fact says 13+23+⋯+n3=(1+2+⋯+n)213+23+⋯+n3=(1+2+⋯+n)2. Use it on a slice to find 93+10393+103 without cubing 99 or 1010 directly. Write the two-cube sum as one stack of cubes minus a shorter stack, then finish.
Show the solution
Take the whole stack of cubes up to 1010 and remove the stack up to 88. What survives is exactly 93+10393+103. By the holding-hands fact each stack is the square of a plain running sum, and those sums are 1+⋯+10=551+⋯+10=55 and 1+⋯+8=361+⋯+8=36. So 93+103=552−362=3025−1296=1729.93+103=552−362=3025−1296=1729​. A pair of cubes became a difference of two squares. 17291729 is famous as the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two different ways.
Practice
Stack up the odd numbers starting from 1, and look at the totals. 11, then 1+3=41+3=4, then 1+3+5=91+3+5=9, then 1+3+5+7=161+3+5+7=16. Every one of those totals is a perfect square, and it never stops. The first nn odd numbers always add up to n2n2. The ancient Greek Pythagoreans drew exactly this picture, building each new square by wrapping an L-shaped strip of dots, called a gnomon, around the previous square, the same L-shape you just saw in this lesson's figure. It is the same pattern you found at the start of this lesson, just run all the way back to the beginning. 🚀
Practice
Add up the first few cubes and look at the totals. 13=113=1, then 13+23=913+23=9, then 13+23+33=3613+23+33=36, then 13+23+33+43=10013+23+33+43=100. Every total is a perfect square, and not a random one. 9=329=32, 36=6236=62, 100=102100=102, and 3,6,103,6,10 are exactly the running sums 1+21+2, 1+2+31+2+3, 1+2+3+41+2+3+4. So a stack of cubes always equals the square of a plain sum, 13+23+⋯+n3=(1+2+⋯+n)213+23+⋯+n3=(1+2+⋯+n)2. The two halves of this lesson, squares and cubes, turn out to be holding hands. 🚀
